role: Staff, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, Air Pollution Control Section
stance_basis: memo explicitly states draft EIS is 'deficient in several respects' and raises extensive air quality concerns requiring additional analysis
summary: R. W. Park, writing on behalf of the Wisconsin DNR Air Pollution Control Section, submitted a detailed intra-department memorandum finding the draft EIS deficient in several respects regarding air quality. Park raised concerns about vehicle emissions, the meteorological effects of Lake Michigan on air pollution dispersion, inadequate air monitoring data, the failure to conduct worst-case air quality calculations, and the broader implications of developing Mitchell Field as a multi-purpose airport. Park's overall position is that the EIS as drafted does not adequately address air quality impacts and requires substantial additional analysis before the project can be approved.
complaint_summary: R. W. Park's memo on behalf of the DNR Air Pollution Control Section finds the draft EIS deficient in addressing local air quality impacts, vehicle emission projections, Lake Michigan meteorological effects on pollution dispersion, mass transit alternatives, air monitoring accuracy, and the need for worst-case calculations along the spur corridor.

statement.text:
The above draft statement has been reviewed by the Air Pollution Control Section and found deficient in several respects. In view of the location of the proposed project in an urban area near the Lake Michigan shoreline, the final EIS should address itself to the following questions:
1. What will the project's impact be on local air quality? A worst case calculation should be done taking into account the current relaxed federal government schedule for emission controls on automobiles. Since the proposed spur would channel traffic to the air terminal parking lot, what effects can be expected there from combining aircraft and automobile emissions?
2. Is it necessary or desirable to develop General Mitchell Field as a multi-purpose airport serving passenger, freight, military, corporate and private aircraft needs all at the same site? If it is necessary to develop a single large airport to serve the Milwaukee area, is Mitchell Field the best site? In view of the rapidly growing megalopolis along the shore of Lake Michigan south of Milwaukee, will it eventually be necessary to develop another large airport in a less congested area farther from the lakeshore to serve the same region?
3. Is the proposed freeway addition the best way to facilitate the movement of future airport users to and from the airfield? Can transportation plans be developed in such a way as to transfer a significant portion of these users from automobiles to mass transit?
4. Is there evidence of an adverse effect on air quality caused by the special meteorological conditions pertaining along the shore of Lake Michigan?
These and less crucial questions are dealt with in more detail below.

Vehicle Emissions
On pages 90 and 107 the draft EIS states that by the time the airport spur is open to traffic, the vehicles using it will be subject to stringent government regulations. This statement is inaccurate because the federal emission limits originally set for 1975 and now postponed until 1976 will apply only to 1976 and later model-year cars. There will still be many older cars on the highways and there is no requirement presently anticipated for retrofitting them with comparable emission control devices. Earlier model-year cars made in the mid 1970's will presumably have control devices designed to bring them into compliance with interim emission standards. However it remains to be seen how reliable the new devices are and how rapidly they deteriorate from their original operating efficiency.
The possibility of further easing of federal emission control regulations or enforcement schedules should also be taken into account. The questions of how soon cars meeting the 1976 standards will actually be available and whether they will in fact maintain the required emission control for 50,000 miles remain in some doubt. In view of these considerations, the EPA prediction of a 25% reduction in carbon monoxide emissions by 1975, mentioned on page 90 of the statement, should be considered highly optimistic.
The emission factors given on page 92 of the statement and used in the calculations on pages 92B and 92C will underrate the emissions from Wisconsin cars because they are based on California cars. California law has predated federal law in requiring increasingly strict emission controls on automobiles. (This does not invalidate the corridor comparisons made on page 92B, however). In addition, the accuracy of any predicted future emission rates depends on the validity of the assumption that planned federal regulations will be successfully implemented and firmly enforced. A more sound approach to predicting emission rates along a new freeway such as the airport spur might be to collect data on the actual trends in emissions along present Milwaukee freeways as emission controlled vehicles come into wider use. These data could then be used to determine the actual improvements to be expected when future vehicle emission regulations go into effect.
Development Which Generates New Traffic
The draft EIS gives projections showing total passenger and aircraft movement at General Mitchell Field more than doubling before 1990. In planning for this sort of rapid expansion, the fact that patterns of development in urban areas can have a marked impact on air quality needs to be taken into account.

No consideration is given in the EIS to the possibility that a maximum use level should be set for Mitchell Field, with some of its functions eventually transferred to other fields. On pages 33 and 34 the report states that expansion of air terminal, air cargo and Air National Guard facilities at the airport are all either underway or expected and it mentions that facilities for corporate and private aircraft are also provided. Could some of these needs be met just as well by smaller airports elsewhere in the region? From the standpoint of air quality, the development of a large multi-purpose airport to serve southeastern Wisconsin is probably less desirable than developing several decentralized airports serving specialized needs because the single large airport will result in a greater concentration of traffic. In addition, smaller airports and airports placed farther from residential areas are more desirable from a noise pollution perspective. The draft EIS states on page 35 that "General Mitchell Field...could not possibly acquire all the land that would be necessary to abate the airport noise problems" and points out that federal regulations will require jet engines to be less noisy in the future. Steps to limit the number of vehicles and aircraft using the airport would also limit the growth of the noise problem.
If heavy passenger traffic eventually made it necessary to build another large airport farther inland from the growing congestion of the lakeshore area, the transportation of air passengers between the two airports might aggravate all traffic related problems including air pollution. If the need for such a facility is anticipated, could its development be planned so as to avoid the increase in air passenger traffic presently projected for Mitchell Field by 1990?
The fact that Mitchell Field lies only three miles from the shore of Lake Michigan may prove to be an important reason for limiting the development of the airport. Recent studies by Cole and Lyons (1) and others raise the possibility that air pollution problems along the shoreline of the Great Lakes may be "greatly magnified by the Lakes" effects on the transport and diffusion of pollutants." As a result Cole and Lyons suggest that policies be adopted which would "reduce automobile traffic within the first four to five miles of the shoreline. Replacement of automobiles by a low pollution mass transit system within the shoreline corridors is one solution. Development that would promote increased traffic close to the lakes should be restricted." The possible effect of Lake Michigan on air pollution in the parts of Milwaukee nearest the shoreline is discussed in the section on local meteorology.
Since the proposed spur will connect to Howell Avenue near the airport terminal, it can be expected to promote development of the businesses established along the edge of the airfield. If the accompanying increase in vehicle traffic on Howell Avenue (already a busy thoroughfare) is rapid enough, the adverse effect on local air quality may be significant.

Mass Transit
The Milwaukee hus system, which in 1951 carried nearly 200 million passengers, today carries barely 50 million passengers per year (2). The draft EIS states that more than 90% of all vehicles entering the passenger terminal area of Mitchell Field are private cars but no steps are proposed to bring about more balance in the modes of transportation used by people desiring access to the airport.
4.
In the calculation of emissions from spur traffic, the ratio of light-duty vehicles to heavy-duty vehicles was assumed to remain unchanged from 1977 to 1990. Since Milwaukee freeways seem to fill to capacity almost as soon as they are opened, consideration should be given to the question of whether, in the absence of specific plans for attracting more riders to mass transit, freeway additions like the airport spur promote an increased dependence on the automobile instead.
Although the favored spur corridor crosses the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul and Pacific Railroad line, future rail transport to the airport is dismissed in a single sentence as not feasible (page 56, paragraph 2). What is the location of the nearest railroad terminal and what are the prospects for shuttle bus or limousine service between it and the airport? The EIS mentions on pages 55-56 a plan for a bus lane adjacent to one stretch of freeway but does not say whether such a lane could be added to the proposed spur.
A significant reduction in vehicle emissions along the spur corridor could be obtained if a sizable fraction of the spur users were transported by mass transit instead of by automobile. For example, if passengers in half of the spur traffic were transferred from cars carrying an average of 1.4 passengers per car to diesel buses, predicted carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon emissions along the spur would be reduced by approximately 48% in 1977 and by about 42% for carbon monoxide and 39% for hydrocarbons in 1990.
The rough calculations on which these figures are based used the California emission factors given on page 92 of the draft EIS and the emission factors for heavy-duty, diesel powered vehicles given on page 3.1.5-2 of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Compilation of Air Pollutant Emission Factors, Second Edition (1973). An average of 30 passengers per bus was assumed. The calculations may underestimate the actual reduction in emissions because the buses would reduce traffic congestion and increase average traffic speed and because the California emission factors are too low for two reasons:

1) they do not reflect the federal government's recent relaxation of their enforcement schedule for emission controls and, 2) controls on California cars have predated controls on cars elsewhere in the country.

In view of the improved air quality and reduced traffic congestion available through the use of mass transit, an airport shuttle service should be considered as an alternative to building at least part of the proposed spur. A shuttle system serving parking facilities for Chicago's O'Hare Field is already under construction. A shuttle plan for Mitchell Field might take the following form, for example.
The high capacity freeway could terminate at the point where it meets the railroad line and transportation the rest of the distance to the airport could be provided by a relatively narrow, at-grade parkway designed for use by an efficient mass transit shuttle service. A commuter depot could be provided at the rail line and automobile parking could be provided at the depot and along the parkway. Parking and shuttle vehicle stops would be arranged to minimize the distance air passengers would have to carry their luggage, and the shuttle vehicle would take them right to the airport terminal building.
With savings in roadway construction costs, more money could be devoted to planting trees along the parkway which would make it more pleasant to use than a freeway with a concrete barrier down the center. Use of the shuttle service could also be encouraged by setting much higher parking fees at the air terminal parking lot than the parkway park-and-ride cost. The availability of shuttle service to the airport at short intervals would, in turn, encourage the development of commuter service on the railroad.
This plan would reduce air pollution along the last mile of travel to the airport because a large number of cars would be replaced by a few mass transit vehicles. Division of parking between the parkway and the air terminal would aid the dispersion of automobile emissions and a reduction rather than an expansion of parking at the terminal might be possible. This would help to avoid some of the complex air pollution problems that can be expected in a large airport parking lot when automobile emissions are combined with aircraft emissions. In addition, the problem of the proposed spur blocking the tower's view of part of one runway would be avoided with a parkway built at-grade.
Local Meteorology
All of the proposed spur sites lie within five miles of the western shore of Lake Michigan in an area where meteorological conditions are influenced by the presence of the lake. Cole and Lyons (1) believe that the environmental impact statement for a project in such an area, in considering impact on air quality, should "include a detailed study of the local air pollution meteorology, including the lake effect." This information is missing from the airport spur draft EIS.

Cole and Lyons state that the influence of the lake on air quality "is most detrimental on spring and summer days when stable lake air flows inland. Adverse dispersion phenomena were found to occur in association with three distinct mesoscale regimes: the lake breeze circulation, gradient onshore flow with strong sunlight and gradient onshore flow with minimal solar radiation."
"In the Chicago-Milwaukee area it is believed that the stable lake air flows onshore on about two-thirds of spring and summer days," according to these researchers. "In all cases, stable onshore flow appears to limit the height of the mixing layer within the first few miles of the lakefront" and the "mixing heights are greatly reduced with increasing proximity to the shoreline."
Since two of the three regimes occur in bright sunshine and on warm days, they appear ideal for the production of photochemical smog from poorly dispersed vehicle emissions of hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides. In addition, air pollution may be aggravated in the case of the lake breeze circulation cells by the recycling of pollutants. These cells develop "when the layer of air over the land is heated relative to the air over the water. On the western shore of Lake Michigan lake breezes develop on about 35% of spring and summer days." These breezes "are best developed on those days when sunlight is the strongest" (1).
The potential for photochemical smog along the lakeshore is further increased by the stabilizing effect of the lakes during the warm season which severely restricts the growth of cumulus clouds overhead. As a result the solar radiation received along the shoreline is considerably stronger than that received several miles inland (1).
The danger of photochemical smog is not limited to days with lake breeze circulation and easterly gradient winds. As Cole and Lyons have pointed out, "the Milwaukee area frequently experiences smoke, haze and odor on afternoons when moderate to strong, south to southwest winds are accompanied by strong sunlight. Under these conditions, an onshore component of wind develops...causing stabilized air to flow several kilometers inland toward a zone of convergence running parallel to the western shoreline of Lake Michigan. Along with the bright sunshine necessary for photochemical smog, this regime would cause pronounced reduction of mixing depth near the shoreline where automobile emissions are concentrated. Secondly, it is likely that pollutants may be channeled along the shoreline by the converging winds, and it is entirely possible that pollutants from automobiles and industries in the Chicago-Gary region may be channeled long distances along the shoreline creating photochemical smog and high particulate concentration as far north as Milwaukee."

The third mesoscale regime identified by Cole and Lyons occurs on overcast days or at night so photochemical smog is not promoted. However the dispersion of low level emissions is more severely restricted in this case than in the other two. A lid of stable inflowing air is produced which can extend inland for tens of miles. Beneath this capping inversion strong mixing is promoted in a shallow turbulent layer. The plumes from low level static sources are trapped in this layer and vertical mixing of pollutants from mobile sources is also limited. This could cause the accumulation of high levels of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen exides from vehicle emissions in the shallow, turbulent layer of air as it moves inland across heavily traveled streets and highways.
Construction which involves the laying of large areas of concrete can itself have an impact on local meteorology. Glider pilots have become familiar with the rising currents of air caused by large parking lots on sunny days, for example. The "heat island" effect found in cities is increased whenever vegetation is replaced by pavement. On days of high pollution the upward-directed thermal radiation emitted by such surfaces is partly absorbed by the blanket of pollutants over a city. "Tart of this radiation is re-emitted downward and...warms the ambient air, a process that tends to increase low-level stability over the city, enhancing the probability of higher pollutant concentrations" (3). Increasing the heat island effect can also be expected to promote lake breeze circulation cells, which depend on the temperature difference between land and lake surfaces. These cells may also hinder the dispersion of pollutants. When plants are present part of the incident solar energy is used for moisture evaporation and ground heating is decreased. It follows that as many trees in the spur corridor should be preserved as possible, with new plantings to replace all trees and shrubs removed, - for reasons both of air quality and aesthetics. The draft EIS does not say whether the spur project includes plans to plant as many new trees and shrubs as are destroyed by the construction.
On a larger scale, the meteorology of southeastern Wisconsin is generally favorable for the dispersion of pollutants. Mixing heights are ususally high and wind conditions favorable. "Periods of stagnation which may trap pollutants in an areas for several days are rare" (4). As a result, High Air Pollution Potential alerts are infrequent. This is misleading, however, because the alerts are based on affected areas of 75,000 square miles or more and episode durations of at least 36 hours. As a result they do not reflect local air pollution problems such as may be caused by lake effects. Such local effects are not taken into account by the dispersion models used in Wisconsin's plans for meeting the national ambient air quality standards. Furthermore, the meteorological data used in the models may not reflect lakeshore conditions and, in particular, the summer mixing depths measured some distance inland may be several times greater than the actual mixing depths in shoreline regions (1).

Air Monitoring
The description of the air quality monitoring program in southeastern Wisconsin in the last paragraph on page 88 of the draft EIS is now inaccurate. The paragraph should be rewritten to include the following information.
Continuous air menitoring in the Southeast Wisconsin Air Quality Control Region was begun at two stations last fall and at four more stations during the summer of 1973. Five of the stations are in Milwaukee and one is in Racine. Each of these stations monitors carbon monoxide, ozone, sulfur oxides and coefficient of haze (a measure of particulates). Only one station is presently equipped to monitor hydrocarbons, and no data has been reported as yet. Earlier attempts to sample nitrogen dioxide gave poor results and monitoring of this pollutant has been discontinued until an acceptable method of sampling becomes available. Only one station reported meteorological data (temperature, dew point, wind direction and wind speed) for July but others will record this information in the future. In addition, a mobile van has been equipped to measure carbon monoxide, ozone, sulfur dioxide and particulates as well as the meteorological data mentioned above.
The nearest monitoring station is 4.8 miles from the Mitchell Field terminal. This station is on the lakefront and may give readings uncharacteristic of conditions near the airport much of the time. The next closest station is 6.4 miles from the terminal. There are plans for setting up two more monitoring stations in Milwaukee during the next several months, the nearest site presently planned being Alverno College, 4.0 miles from the terminal.
These facilities will all be supervised by the Department of Natural Resources through its district office in Milwaukee. The Milwaukee County Department of Air Pollution will not be involved in enforcing air quality standards along the airport spur as indicated on page 10 of the statement because the Department of Natural Resources will have taken over the responsibilities of this agency by 1975.
The Southeast Wisconsin Air Quality Control Region has the most extensive air pollution problem in the state. As a result Priority I has been assigned in this region for the monitoring of oxidants, particulates and (as soon as an acceptable method becomes available) nitrogen oxides. In mentioning this on page 89, the draft EIS did not make it clear that these priorities apply only to the Southeast District.
The Air Pollution Problem
The oxidant readings from the six continuous monitoring stations for July and August of this year clearly show that this pollutant is a problem in southeastern Wisconsin. On July 18 and 19 the station in

Racine and four of the five stations in Milwaukee recorded hourly averages for ozone in excess of the National Arbient Air Quality Standard maximum one-hour oxidant concentration of .08 ppm. Federal law requires that this standard, by the surmer of 1975, not be exceeded more than once a year. The lowest readings were at the station farthest from the lakefront. At four locations on July 18 and at three locations on July 19 a level of .4 ppm-hours was exceeded for four consecutive hours. This level would have been high enough to precipitate an air pollution "alert" if the concentrations had been expected to remain at these levels for 12 or more hours or increase in the absence of control actions. Some of the hourly average readings exceeded .2 ppm. Levels above the federal standard were again recorded on several days in August.
Carbon monoxide levels were also in excess of federal air quality standards at one station in downtown Milwaukee on July 18. An eight-hour average concentration of over 10 ppm was measured. The eight-hour maximum concentration to be attained by 1975 (not to be exceeded more than once a year) is 9 ppm. Hence it can no longer be said, as stated on pages 89 and 90 of the draft EIS, that monitoring data indicate that air standards for carbon monoxide are being met in the Milwaukee area. The statement that only downtown Milwaukee is known to have oxidant levels above the air standard is also incorrect. High levels have been measured in Racine, as mentioned above, and also near Poynette where concentrations up to .24 ppm have been found.
In view of the present failure to meet air quality standards in the Milwaukee area, it does not appear adequate to simply compare the areawide pollutant loads produced by airport traffic with and without construction of the airport spur. The impact of the spur on air quality both along its right of way and at associated parking facilities needs to be determined. Data on existing air quality in the area need to be utilized and measurements of pollutant levels along the present I-94 and at the air terminal parking lot would also be helpful. Furthermore, in view of the large increase in air traffic being planned for, aircraft emissions should be taken into account.
A Department of Natural Resources study estimated that the total aircraft emissions at General Mitchell Field during 1971 were as follows:

Recently installed emission controls have resulted in a sharp decrease in particulate emissions from aircraft but current emission factors reflect an increase in emissions of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides. With a rapid increase in the number of aircraft using the airfield and with a probable increase in idling times as the field becomes more heavily used, these emissions, added to the emissions of vehicular traffic flowing to and from the airport, may pose a problem, especially in any congested parking area near the terminal. In view of the large tonnage of nitrogen oxides generated by the aircraft, it would seem advisable to include a calculation of vehicular nitrogen oxide emissions in the EIS.
The calculations on pages 92-92C of the statement do not make it clear how much traffic will be noving in the airport area in addition to that using the airport spur and no comment is made on how this traffic can be expected to change in volume between the opening of the spur and 1990.
Local traffic should be taken into account because the air quality near a particular roadway will depend on the total traffic using it.
Another consideration not taken into account in these calculations is the fact that traffic dispersion aids in the dispersion of air pollutants. The five possible corridors and the "no build" alternative are compared on the basis of total tons of carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons emitted per day by the estimated traffic desiring access to the airport from the present interstate system. However it is assumed for corridors 1 and 4 that a portion of this traffic will take a route to the terminal other than the proposed spur, and with the no build alternative the traffic is dispersed over four different, partially overlapping routes. Hence in terms of local pollutant concentrations, these alternatives are not strictly comparable to the other three corridors and, in particular, the favored corridor 5 is not strictly comparable to the no build alternative.
A "worst case" calculation should be carried out for the air quality along the airport spur. Since the most stringent emission controls are not required on new automobiles until 1976, the vorst case might occur soon after the spur opens, during peak traffic flow. If it is still possible that the spur will be open by late 1975, a calculation should be done for this year. The traffic data needed would include the projected peak hourly flow, the time at which it occurs, the associated average traffic speed and the heavy-duty vehicle mix broken down into gasoline powered and diesel powered vehicles. The expected eight-hour traffic maximum would also be useful. In addition, a calculation should be made for off-peak traffic conditions. A liaison meeting between several staff members from the Department of Transportation and the Department of Natural Resources Air Pollution Control Section was held on September 6 to discuss such calculations.

In the absence of detailed air quality data and calculations for the airport area, some general comments can be made. To the extent that the proposed spur provides for smooth, rapid flow of traffic to the airport and relieves congestion on other heavily traveled streets in the area, it should improve air quality. However to the extent that the spur and related development at and around the airport lead to more intensive use of the area, with a significantly heavier total traffic flow, an eventual deterioration of air quality may be caused. The present oxidant problem being experienced in the Milwaukee area suggests that steps are needed to reduce emissions of hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides since these pollutants are known to react to produce ozone in the presence of sunlight. Steps may also be needed to reduce carbon monoxide emissions in order to meet the federal air quality standards. Efforts to improve air quality in the increasingly congested lakeshore region may ultimately require that limits be placed on the growth of total vehicle flow around major traffic generators such as the airport.
References
(1) Cole, H. S. and W. A. Lyons, "The impact of the Great Lakes on the air quality of urban shoreline areas; some practical applications with regard to air pollution control policy and environmental decision making." Proc. 15th Conf. Great Lakes Res., Internat. Assoc. Great Lakes Res., 436-463 (1972).
(2) "Urban Bus Systems", The Wisconsin Taxpayer, 41, 1-9, August, 1973.
(3) Peterson, J. T. "The Climate of Cities: A Survey of Recent Literature," U. S. EPA, page 16, October 1969.
(4) "Monitoring and control of regional air pollution; southeastern Wisconsin," Inst. for Environmental Studies, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Report 4, April, 1973.
